title: Improved Online Conformal Prediction via Strongly Adaptive Online Learning
research_question: Can online conformal prediction be made strongly adaptive so that prediction sets maintain useful coverage and efficiency across localized time intervals under changing or arbitrarily shifting data distributions?
methodology: The authors formulate Strongly Adaptive Online Conformal Prediction (SAOCP), a meta-algorithm that maintains multiple finite-lifetime online-learning experts operating on different active intervals, and instantiate those experts with Scale-Free Online Gradient Descent (SF-OGD). They prove strongly adaptive regret and coverage guarantees, including a near-optimal regret rate simultaneously over all interval lengths. Empirical evaluation covers multi-horizon forecasting on M4 and NN5 time-series datasets and image classification under sudden and gradual corruption shifts on TinyImageNet/TinyImageNet-C and ImageNet/ImageNet-C, using coverage, prediction-set size or width, local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret.

key_findings.finding: SAOCP achieves strongly adaptive regret of order approximately sqrt(k) up to logarithmic factors simultaneously for every interval length k, whereas the compared FACI guarantee can be tuned to a comparable rate for a particular interval length but not all lengths simultaneously.

SF-OGD has a distribution-free empirical coverage-error bound that converges to zero, while SAOCP receives a distribution-free bound for a randomized expert-selection variant and stronger interval-wise coverage guarantees under additional distributional regularity assumptions.

Across the three M4 forecasting datasets, SAOCP maintained global coverage near the 0.9 target and consistently obtained the best or second-best interval width, local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret across the tested base predictors.
Under sudden and gradual image-distribution shifts, SAOCP and SF-OGD kept local coverage closest to the 0.9 target, with the advantage most pronounced around abrupt change points.

Directly predicting the conformal radius, as done by SF-OGD and SAOCP, was empirically more robust than quantile-style parameterizations in several cases where the underlying forecasting model had relatively high prediction error.

limitations: The principal distribution-free coverage theorem for SAOCP is stated for a randomized variant that samples an expert rather than for the deterministic weighted-radius form used as the main algorithm.
The strongest interval-wise coverage result requires additional regularity assumptions and depends on temporal variation in the true quantiles.
The theoretical formulation assumes nested prediction sets and a bounded maximum radius parameter.
Empirical evaluation is confined to time-series forecasting and image corruption benchmarks rather than free-form generative models.
The experiments use specific benchmark shift processes, so they do not exhaust the range of non-stationary or adversarial changes that could occur in deployment.
The paper addresses calibration through prediction-set coverage rather than evidence completeness, omission detection, or selective abstention for long-form text.
raw_claims: SAOCP manages multiple experts whose active intervals are localized in time.
At most logarithmically many experts are active at a given time when the lifetime multiplier is constant.
SAOCP attains a near-optimal strongly adaptive regret rate simultaneously over all interval lengths.
SF-OGD's empirical coverage error converges toward the target without distributional assumptions.
The forecasting evaluation uses 5,111 time series across M4 and NN5.
Forecasting metrics include global coverage, median interval width, worst-case local coverage error, and strongly adaptive regret.
SAOCP outperforms the main adaptive baselines on localized coverage and regret across the reported M4 experiments.
Image experiments include both abrupt and gradual changes in corruption severity.
SAOCP and SF-OGD react more effectively to image-distribution change points than the slower-adapting baselines.
The authors provide experimental code in a public repository.
